analysis.one_liner: Weakens the consumer financial regulator: commission instead of director, no independent funding, bank regulators can veto its rules.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 232–182 on February 27, 2014, with 222 of 231 Republicans in favor, but the Senate never voted and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have replaced the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's single director with a five-member commission, ended the agency's independent funding from the Federal Reserve and subjected it to annual congressional appropriations capped at $300 million, and required consumer permission before the agency collected personal financial data [S4]. Its largest change would have made it much easier to block the agency's rules: a council dominated by banking regulators could stay or strike down any rule on a simple majority vote, using a far easier standard than today's system-wide risk test [S3]. It also repealed the agency's exclusive authority to write rules under federal consumer financial law [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Banks, credit card issuers, mortgage lenders, and high-cost lenders facing Consumer Financial Protection Bureau rules and enforcement. Any of the agency's rules could be stayed or thrown out by a simple majority of the Financial Stability Oversight Council, a body where banking regulators hold most of the seats [S3][S5]. The agency's money would flow through annual appropriations, where affected industries focus their lobbying, instead of coming automatically from the Federal Reserve [S4]. Repealing the agency's exclusive rulemaking authority would open consumer rules to influence from other regulators friendlier to industry [S5].

how_it_helps.text: Lowers the vote needed to stay or set aside a consumer protection rule from two-thirds of the Financial Stability Oversight Council to a simple majority, and requires the Council to kill any rule it deems 'inconsistent with the safe and sound operations of U.S. financial institutions' — replacing the current test that a rule must threaten the entire banking system or financial stability.

Ends the agency's independent funding drawn from the Federal Reserve and replaces it with annual congressional appropriations of $300 million, giving Congress and the industries that lobby it an annual choke point over the agency's budget.
Replaces the single Director with a five-member commission and repeals the agency's exclusive authority to write rules under federal consumer financial law, dispersing control over consumer rules.

Bars the agency from requesting, obtaining, or using consumers' nonpublic personal financial information without the consumer's advance permission, and strips its exemption from the Right to Financial Privacy Act.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary consumers who rely on the rules the agency writes and enforces — checking account and credit card customers, mortgage borrowers, servicemembers targeted by payday lenders near bases — would face a regulator whose rules can be stayed or struck before they take effect and whose funding must survive the annual appropriations fight. The failed motion to recommit specifically sought to preserve the agency's ability to warn consumers about data breaches, protect servicemembers from payday lenders, and act on ATM and private student loan fees [S7][S8].
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers using banks, cards, and loans

drawbacks.text: The core change makes consumer rules far easier to block: a simple majority of a banking-regulator-dominated council could stay a rule immediately and set aside any rule deemed merely inconsistent with banks' own safe operations, instead of the current two-thirds vote and system-wide risk standard.

Subjecting the agency to annual appropriations and repealing its exclusive rulemaking authority would make its budget and its rulebook dependent on congressional action each year, where regulated industries concentrate their lobbying.

The good-faith case for parts of the bill: a single director whose funding bypasses the appropriations process holds unusual unchecked power, and the privacy section responds to a real practice — the agency collecting large volumes of consumers' nonpublic financial data without their permission.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The accountability and privacy arguments have some substance — the single-director, self-funded structure was genuinely unusual. But the bill's main effect is not accountability; it is to make almost any consumer rule blockable by a majority of banking regulators using a much weaker standard than the law required, and to put the agency's funding in the annual appropriations gauntlet. For consumers, the costs of a weakened regulator — weaker mortgage, credit card, and payday lending rules — outweigh the governance improvements.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it on a mostly party-line vote, but the Senate, then run by Democrats, received it in March 2014 and never brought it to a vote, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: The House Committee on Financial Services marked up the bill and ordered it reported by a 32–25 vote, and it was placed on the Union Calendar in February 2014.

On February 27, 2014, the House considered the bill under a rule from the Rules Committee, adopted an amendment in the nature of a substitute converting it into the Financial Product Safety Commission structure, and passed it 232–182 (Roll no. 85).

A Democratic motion to recommit with instructions — to preserve the agency's authority on data-breach warnings, servicemember protection from payday lenders, and ATM and private student loan fees — failed 194–223 (Roll no. 84), with 193 of 199 Democrats voting yes and all but one of 231 Republicans voting no.
The Senate received the bill on March 4, 2014, and the action record shows no further Senate action through the end of the 113th Congress in January 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau came out ahead: because the bill died in the Senate, the agency kept its single-director structure, its independent Federal Reserve funding, its exclusive rulemaking authority, and the high bar for overturning its rules. Banks and lenders facing the agency's rules did not get the veto power this bill would have handed them.

sides.party_line_note: House Republicans voted 222–0 for passage, joined by 10 of 199 Democrats; on the motion to recommit, 193 of 199 Democrats voted yes against all but one of 231 Republicans.

industries.note: The bill hands banking regulators on the Financial Stability Oversight Council a simple-majority veto over any consumer rule, using a standard tied to banks' own interests rather than system-wide risk, and repeals the consumer agency's exclusive rulemaking power. Consumers would bear the cost through weaker mortgage, credit card, and deposit account rules.

The failed motion to recommit specifically sought to preserve the agency's ability to protect servicemembers from predatory payday lending near military bases, which indicates what a weakened agency would struggle to do.

industries.industry: Companies the agency supervises (data and enforcement targets)
industries.note: The privacy provisions require consumer permission before the agency collects nonpublic personal financial information, restricting the data the agency can use to spot and prove abuses in markets like credit reporting and debt collection.
